Session 1
The idea of DP
Overlapping subproblems · Memoization · Tables · Grid paths
Why DP · 8 minutes
Fibonacci: a simple recursion that explodes
F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)
Naive recursion
3.3 × 10^8
calls to compute F(40).
Remember each value
41
different subproblems F(0) to F(40). Each needs one addition.
Demo 1 · Watch the calls
The call tree of fib(5)
Four ideas · 12 minutes
What every DP is made of
1
State
What does dp[i] mean? Say it in one sentence.
2
Recurrence
How does a state follow from smaller states?
3
Base cases
The states you know without computing.
4
Order and answer
Compute smaller states first, then read the answer.
Cost = number of states × work per state. DP applies when subproblems overlap and the best answer is built from best answers of smaller problems.
Two styles
Top-down and bottom-up
Top-down: memoization
long long memo[N]; bool seen[N]; long long fib(int n) {     if (n <= 1) return n;     if (seen[n]) return memo[n];     seen[n] = true;     return memo[n] = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); }
Keep the recursion, cache results. Only needed states are computed.
Bottom-up: table
f[0] = 0; f[1] = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++)     f[i] = f[i-1] + f[i-2]; // answer: f[n]
Fill a table in increasing order. No recursion, so no stack depth problem.
A first real DP · 15 minutes
Counting paths on a grid
Problem
An n × m grid, some cells blocked. Move only right or down from the top-left to the bottom-right cell. Count the paths.
Think about the last move
A path to cell (i, j) arrives from above or from the left. So the paths to (i, j) are the paths to (i−1, j) plus the paths to (i, j−1).
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]
Demo 2 · Watch the table fill
Grid paths with two blocked cells
C++ implementation
Grid paths
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)     for (int j = 0; j < m; j++) {         if (blocked[i][j]) { dp[i][j] = 0; continue; }         if (i == 0 && j == 0) { dp[i][j] = 1; continue; }         dp[i][j] = (i ? dp[i-1][j] : 0) + (j ? dp[i][j-1] : 0);     } cout << dp[n-1][m-1];
Counts grow fast: use long long, or take the result modulo 10^9 + 7 when the statement asks for it.
The recipe
The same four ideas, two problems
Fibonacci
Grid paths
State
f[i] = F(i)
dp[i][j] = paths to cell (i, j)
Recurrence
f[i] = f[i-1] + f[i-2]
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]
Base cases
f[0] = 0, f[1] = 1
dp[0][0] = 1, blocked cells = 0
Order
increasing i
rows top to bottom, left to right
Answer
f[n]
dp[n-1][m-1]
Cost
O(n)
O(n · m)
Pitfalls
Three classic DP bugs
01
Weak state
If dp[i] cannot decide the next step, the state is missing information. Add a dimension.
02
Missing base case
Reading dp[-1] or an unset cell gives garbage. List base cases first.
03
Wrong order, overflow
Compute a cell only after its inputs. Counts need long long or a modulus.
Review
Three ideas to keep
Overlap
The same subproblem appears many times. Solve it once.
State and recurrence
Say what dp means, then express it with smaller states.
States × transitions
That product is the running time.

Session 2
Classic DP problems
Minimum coins · 0/1 knapsack · Choosing a method
Minimum coins · 12 minutes
Fewest coins for an amount
Problem
Coins of values c1, …, ck, unlimited supply. Find the fewest coins that sum to S.
The greedy trap
Coins 1, 3, 4 and S = 6. Largest first gives 4 + 1 + 1, three coins. The best is 3 + 3, two coins.
dp[0] = 0, dp[x] = min over coins c ≤ x of ( dp[x - c] + 1 )
State: dp[x] is the fewest coins for amount x. Try each coin as the last one.
Demo 3 · Watch the table fill
Minimum coins for amount 6
C++ implementation
Minimum coins
dp[0] = 0; for (int x = 1; x <= S; x++) {     dp[x] = INF;     for (int c : coins)         if (x >= c && dp[x - c] + 1 < dp[x]) { dp[x] = dp[x - c] + 1; from[x] = c; } } for (int x = S; x > 0; x -= from[x]) print(from[x]);     // reconstruct
Cost O(S × k). If dp[S] is still INF, the amount cannot be made.
0/1 knapsack · 14 minutes
Pick items under a weight limit
Problem
n items with weight w and value v, and a knapsack of capacity W. Take each item at most once to maximize the total value.
State and recurrence
dp[i][c] is the best value using the first i items with capacity c. Item i is either skipped or taken.
dp[i][c] = max( dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c-w] + v )
Demo 4 · Watch the table fill
0/1 knapsack, capacity 7
C++ implementation
0/1 knapsack
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)     for (int c = 0; c <= W; c++) {         dp[i][c] = dp[i-1][c];                                       // skip item i         if (c >= w[i]) dp[i][c] = max(dp[i][c], dp[i-1][c-w[i]] + v[i]);  // take item i     } cout << dp[n][W];
Cost O(n × W) time and memory. Row i reads only row i − 1.
Space trick
One array is enough
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)     for (int c = W; c >= w[i]; c--)              // descending: each item once         dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]);
Going downward keeps dp[c − w] from the previous item. Going upward would reuse item i again: that is the unbounded knapsack.
Where states come from
Four common DP shapes
PREFIX
dp[i]
Best answer ending at or within the first i elements. Example: longest increasing subsequence.
TWO PREFIXES
dp[i][j]
Prefixes of two sequences. Example: longest common subsequence.
GRID
dp[i][j]
Cell coordinates. Example: paths or minimum cost.
CAPACITY
dp[i][c]
Items and a resource. Example: knapsack, subset sum.
Choosing a method
DP, greedy or backtracking?
Backtracking
Try everything. Exponential, but pruning can help. Use when n is tiny.
Dynamic programming
Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Polynomial in the number of states.
Greedy
A local choice is provably safe. Fast, but needs a proof. Coins 1, 3, 4 break it.
Pitfalls
What goes wrong in classic DPs
01
Loop direction
Descending for 0/1 knapsack, ascending for unlimited coins.
02
INF arithmetic
INF + 1 can overflow. Pick an INF you can safely add to.
03
No path stored
To print the solution, store the choice or recompute it backwards.

At the board · Round 1
One state, simple recurrence
CARD 1 · WARM-UP
Stairs
Climb n ≤ 10^6 stairs, 1 or 2 steps at a time. Count the ways modulo 10^9 + 7.
Hint: f[i] = f[i-1] + f[i-2].
CARD 2 · EASY
Cheapest path
A grid of costs. Move right or down. Find the minimum total cost from top-left to bottom-right.
Hint: dp = cost + min(up, left).
CARD 3 · EASY
Maximum subarray
Given n numbers, find the largest sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray.
Hint: dp[i] is the best sum ending at i.
At the board · Round 2
Tables with a resource
CARD 4 · EASY
Ways to make change
Unlimited coins. Count the ways to make S, where the order of coins does not matter.
Hint: coins in the outer loop.
CARD 5 · MEDIUM
Subset sum
n ≤ 100 numbers, S ≤ 10^4. Can some subset have sum S?
Hint: boolean dp[c], descending loop.
CARD 6 · MEDIUM
Increasing subsequence
Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, n ≤ 2000.
Hint: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j], j < i, a[j] < a[i].
